name: Tausug
confidence_why: Ashley & Ashley 1963 (Parang, Jolo) and Peneyra 1992 (Jolo town) report predictable final stress, but Tan 1967 (Siasi, a native-speaker phonology) and Soderberg, Ashley & Olson 2012 (a Jolo speaker) report penultimate stress, and with both placements attested for Jolo itself and the 1963 paper already noting a penult pitch rise beside final stress, the sources agree only that stress is non-contrastive and falls at the right edge of the word.

catalog_quote: [Ashley & Ashley 1963 sec. 5.1] The writers consider stress to be non phonemic in Tausug because the occurrence of stress is predictable falling on the last syllable of a word. ... Isolation forms sometimes seem to be stressed on the penult and at other times the same form seems to be stressed on the ultima. ... Within a context, however, stress falls only on the last syllable of a word. On many words there is a nonphonemic rise in pitch over the penultimate syllable which makes it hard to hear the final stress. [Tan 1967 sec. 6.1 p.162] When both, however, occurs in words of more than one syllable, the stronger stress is always observed to fall on the penultimate (second to the last) syllable. ... At times some individual words may seem to have the primary stress on the penult and sometimes on the ultima. This does not, however, change the meaning of words. ... This observation is true…

new_statements.quote: Stress in Tausug is non-phonemic; it normally falls on the last syllable of a word. Length is phonemic; it contrasts with its absence in words like /qirpun/ 'shrimp' and /qipun/ 'tooth'. Length is marked by a colon. The other suprasegmental features of pitch and juncture are not included in this study.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text) and. Sec. 1.2 'Suprasegmental features' reads word for word: 'Stress in Tausug is non-phonemic; it normally falls on the last syllable of a word. Length is phonemic; it contrasts with its absence in words like /qirpun/ 'shrimp' and /qipun/ 'tooth'. Length is marked by a colon. The other suprasegmental features of pitch and juncture are not included in this study.' Both text layers agree. Sec. 1.0 states the data 'were elicited from the dialect of Tausug spoken in the town of Jolo', so the work is about Tausug (Jolo dialect). Reading fixed: final syllable is the right fixed-list fit (non-contrastive, normally last syllable); no secondary stress, no exceptions beyond '…
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Tausug with an empty rule field and there are no existing statements; Peneyra supplies a placement (final, non-phonemic) where the catalog records none. Data are from the Jolo-town dialect (sec. 1.0).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is not contrastive; it normally falls on the last syllable of the word. Vowel length is phonemic and independent of stress (marked with a colon).
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the hedge 'normally' is the only qualification. Pitch and juncture are explicitly left out of the study.
new_statements.identity_note: Peneyra 1992 states (sec. 1.0) that her data were elicited from the dialect of Tausug spoken in the town of Jolo. Zorc 1977 (held by the project) distinguishes Jolo Tausug (contrastive accent lost) from Palawan Tausug (historical contrastive accent retained), so the fixed: final syllable / non-phonemic reading is specifically for Jolo Tausug. The Reid 1971 open copy is the Ilongot (Kakiduge:n Bugkalut) page, not Tausug.

new_statements.citation: Reid, Lawrence Andrew (1971). Philippine minor languages: word lists and phonologies. [Honolulu]: University of Hawaii Press. xii+239 pp.
new_statements.check: reported on verification, not yet confirmed
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Reid 1971, Philippine minor languages, has a Tausug entry: no. 43, 'Tausug (Tsg.)', p. 43, 'List supplied by Seymour Ashley', phonological data from Ashley, 'The phonemes of Tausug', PPL 1: 7-17 (1963) -- shown by archive. Reid's phonology pages for other languages carry one-line suprasegmental notes ('Stress', 'Stress (not marked on list)', 'Vowel length', 'Stress unanalyzed'; seen in snippets, language not attributable), so p. 43 may carry such a note for Tausug; it could not be read because the scan is lending-restricted and HathiTrust is search-only. Not a new work; the listed work's Tausug page is simply unopened. Ashley 1963 'The phonemes of Tausug' is a lead the parent may want, not…

readall_conflicts: No disagreement between the two listed works (only Peneyra says anything). Peneyra 1992 (Jolo dialect): stress non-phonemic, normally final; length phonemic. Among files already held by the project from the compilation of 9/16 (not in this works list, checked by a full-text search for stress/accent): Zorc 1977, Bisayan Dialects, sec. 8.10.1 pp. 217-218 says contact with Samal 'has apparently resulted in the loss of such contrastive accent in Tsg on Jolo, while Tsg on Palawan maintains the historical accent patterns' -- consistent with Peneyra's 'non-phonemic' for Jolo but implying a contrastive (lexical) accent system in Palawan Tausug; and the SIL 1979 Southern Gateway phrase book (lines 865-866, p. 23) says 'Stress is not entirely predictable; the best guide is to give even stress to all syllables', a mild tension with Peneyra's predictable final placement. The prior log records Hassan/Ashley/Ashley 1994 and Lobel 2013 as silent on Tausug stress.

audit.reasoning: Quote check: every segment of the deciding quotation is present verbatim at the stated locators in the text we hold layers (Ashley 1963 p.14; Tan 1967 p.162 with fn.47; Soderberg et al. 2012 p.363).
